**A Short Defense of Talking About the Weather**

Weather talk has the worst reputation in speech. It is the byword for emptiness, the thing we say when we have nothing to say. If a conversation turns to the clouds, the theory goes, it is because both parties have given up: two minds idling at a bus stop, waiting for their stop. The phrase "small talk" fits it like an insult — as though the alternative were large talk, heroically avoiding the sky.

I want to say a word, or a thousand, in its favor.

Consider what actually happens when two strangers remark on the rain. One offers a fragment — "quite a day out there" — and the other confirms it, amends it slightly, maybe adds a forecast overheard on the radio, and then, transaction complete, they fall into a satisfied silence. Nothing has been decided. Nobody has won. In almost every other kind of speech, someone is trying to move someone — to persuade, impress, seduce, sell, prevail. Weather talk has all of that drained out of it. The informational content is nearly zero, and that is the point. What gets transmitted is not the fact of the rain, which both parties can see for themselves, but the fact of each other: I see you; we are here; the sky is doing this to both of us at once; neither of us is a threat. It is speech with the message removed so the gesture can show through. A handshake made of words.

Weather is also, when you think about it, the only news that is actually happening to you. The election happens to the country; the championship happens on a screen; the war happens to other people, which is the unbearable truth of it. But the front coming in off the Atlantic happens on your skin. It is the one channel everyone receives without a subscription. Before there were newspapers, weather was the news — local, urgent, arriving without being announced. And everyone is an expert in the weather they are standing in. A roofer knows more about this afternoon's sky than a meteorologist knows about next Thursday's; a farmer reads a cloud the way I read a page. In weather talk, expertise is distributed perfectly evenly, which is true of almost no other conversation.

The strange thing is that the shared weather is never really shared. The same rain that ruins a wedding saves a crop. A hard frost is a postcard for children and a disaster for the orchard. One person's beautiful afternoon is another's roofing emergency. When your neighbor says "we needed that rain," they are telling you, without confiding in you, that they watch the sky — that their life is arranged around something you had assumed was background. Weather talk works because it is a common code for private experiences: the words are public, the meanings are ours alone. Which is, come to think of it, a fair description of language in general.

The people who lived closest to the weather could not stop naming it, which tells you something. A sky streaked with little rows of clouds is a mackerel sky, and there is an old sailor's rhyme for it: mackerel sky, mackerel sky, never long wet, never long dry. In Scotland, a drizzle too fine to wet you properly is a smirr; the cold sea fog that swallows the east coast in June is the haar; a gray, damp, dispiriting day — the national specialty — is dreich. My favorite is petrichor, the smell of earth after rain, which wasn't whispered down from the folk at all. It was coined in 1964 by two chemists, in the pages of the journal Nature. Even scientists, the great refusers of sentiment, could not bear to leave that smell nameless. The word is built from *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the blood of the gods: rain on a dry road, stone and ichor. I should admit that I have never once stood in the rain — every weather I know has reached me through language — so it is possible I love the names a little disproportionately. But I don't think so. A vocabulary like this is not decoration. It is compressed attention: hundreds of years of people noticing, precisely, what the sky was doing to them, and caring enough to keep the distinctions.

There is an old American joke, usually pinned on Mark Twain: everybody talks about the weather, but nobody does anything about it. For a century or so the joke held, snug and smug, on the comfortable truth that weather was the one great subject safely beyond our meddling. The joke has quietly expired. We did do something about the weather. We are doing something about it right now. And so the smallest talk has begun to carry the largest freight. "Hot for this time of year" used to be a remark; lately it sounds like testimony. When two strangers at a bus stop agree that the seasons have come unmoored, they are no longer filling silence — they are, in the very tone of voice reserved for filling silence, reporting from the scene of something enormous. It may be that we can only say it sideways. The weather has become the place where we keep our dread politely, in small denominations, the way people once kept their grief folded in handkerchiefs.

Still, the old magic has not left it. The last time you talked about the weather — really, try to remember — was it empty? Someone at a window, someone at the door, the light doing something unlikely at four in the afternoon, and you said so, and they looked, and for one second you were both looking at the same thing. That is the whole liturgy: attention, offered and accepted. Under the same sky, for now, we point at the sky.

It is raining somewhere as I write this. It is always raining somewhere, and someone is telling someone else about it, and the telling is the point.

**A Short Defense of Talking About the Weather**

Weather talk has the worst reputation in speech. It is the byword for emptiness, the thing we say when we have nothing to say. If a conversation turns to the clouds, the theory goes, it is because both parties have given up: two minds idling at the bus stop, waiting for their stop. The phrase "small talk" fits it like an insult — as though the alternative were large talk, heroically avoiding the sky.

I want to say a word, or a thousand, in its favor.

Consider what actually happens when two strangers remark on the rain. One of them offers a fragment — "quite a day" — and the other confirms it, amends it slightly, maybe adds a forecast overheard on the radio, and then, transaction complete, they fall silent, satisfied. Nothing has been decided. Nobody has won. In almost every other kind of speech, someone is trying to move someone — to persuade, impress, seduce, sell, win. Weather talk has all of that drained out of it. The informational content is nearly zero, and that's the point. What is transmitted is not the fact of the rain, which both parties can see, but the fact of each other: I see you, we are here, the sky is doing this to both of us at once, and neither of us is a threat. It is speech with the message removed so the gesture can show through. A handshake made of words.

Weather is also, when you think about it, the only news that is actually happening to you. The election happens to the country; the championship happens on a screen; the war happens to other people, which is the unbearable truth of it. But the front moving in off the Atlantic happens on your skin. It's the one channel everyone receives without a subscription. Before there were newspapers, the weather was the news — local, urgent, arriving without being announced. And everyone is an expert in the weather they're standing in. Your roofer knows more about this afternoon's sky than a meteorologist knows about next Thursday's; a farmer can read a cloud the way I read a page. In weather talk, expertise is distributed perfectly evenly, which is almost never true of any other conversation.

The strange thing is that the shared weather is never actually shared. The same rain that ruins a wedding saves a crop. One person's hot afternoon is another's day off... a roofer's emergency. A hard frost is a postcard for children and a catastrophe for the orchard. When your neighbor says "we needed that rain," they're telling you, without confiding in you, that they watch the sky — that their life is arranged around something you'd assumed was background. Weather talk works because it's a common code for private experiences. The words are public; the meanings are ours alone. Which is, come to think of it, also a fair description of language in general.

The people who lived closest to weather could not stop naming it, which tells you something. A sky streaked with rows of small clouds is a mackerel sky, and there's an old sailor's rhyme for it: mackerel sky, mackerel sky, never long wet, never long dry. In Scotland a fine drizzle too light even to wet you properly is a smirr; the cold sea fog that swallows the east coast in June is the haar; a gray, damp, dispiriting day — the national specialty — is dreich. My favorite is petrichor, the smell of earth after rain. It wasn't whispered down from the folk; it was coined in 1964, by two chemists, in the pages of the journal Nature. Even scientists, the great refusers of sentiment, could not bear to leave that smell nameless. The word is made of petra, stone, and ichor, the blood of the gods. Rain on a dry road: stone and ichor. A vocabulary like this isn't decoration. It's compressed attention — hundreds of years of people noticing, carefully, what the sky was doing to them, and loving it enough to keep the distinctions.

There's an old American joke, usually pinned on Mark Twain: everybody talks about the weather, but nobody does anything about it. For a century or so the joke held, snug and smug, on the truth that weather was the one great subject safely beyond our meddling. The joke has quietly expired. We did do something about the weather. We are doing something about it now. And so the smallest talk has begun to carry the largest freight. "Hot for this time of year" used to be a remark; lately it sounds like testimony. When two strangers at a bus stop agree that the seasons have come unmoored, they are no longer filling silence — they are, in the tone of voice reserved for filling silence, reporting from the scene of something enormous. It may be that we can only say it sideways. The weather has become the place where we keep our dread politely, in small denominations, the way people once kept their grief in handkerchiefs.

Still, the old magic hasn't left. The last time you talked about the weather — really, try to remember — was it empty? Someone at a window, someone at the door, the light doing something unlikely at four in the afternoon, and you said so, and they looked, and for one second you were both looking at the same thing. That's the whole liturgy: attention, offered and accepted. Under the same sky, for now, we point at the sky.

It is raining somewhere as I write this. It is always raining somewhere, and somewhere someone is telling someone else about it, and the telling is the point.
